questions.html: Suppose that $S$ and $T$ are sets. Which of the following first-order logic statements are translations of the statement " $S$ is not a subset of $T$ ?" Check all that apply.
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Selected solution (score: 19)

Detailed Video Solution: Detailed Video Explanation with Complete Analysis (with Complete Analysis) 

  • If we do it directly by intuition, then if S is not a subset of T then there is definitely some element in S which is not in T 

            $\textup{}\therefore \exists x (x \in S \wedge x \notin T)$

  • It can also be done by writing FOL expression for ‘S is a subset of T’ and then negating it : 

            $\sim \forall x(x \in S\rightarrow x\in T) \\ = \exists x\sim(x\in S\rightarrow x\in T) \\ = \exists x(x\in S\wedge x\notin T) \\ = \exists x(x \in S-T) \\$

  • All this is equivalent to : $S - T\neq \phi$

Let $
R_{1} \text { and } R_{2} \text { be relations on a set } A \text {. }
$

Consider the following statements:

M: if $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ are both reflexive, then so is $R_{1} \cup R_{2}$.

N: if $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ are both symmetric, then so is $R_{1} \cup R_{2}$.

Which of the above statements is/are true?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 5)

(a) Prove that if $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ are both reflexive, then so is $R_{1} \cup R_{2}$.

Proof. Suppose that $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ are both reflexive and let $a \in A$. Then, since $R_{1}$ is reflexive, we have that $(a, a) \in R_{1}$, which means that $(a, a) \in R_{1} \cup R_{2}$.

(b) Prove that if $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ are both symmetric, then so is $R_{1} \cup R_{2}$.

Proof. Suppose that $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ are both symmetric and let $(a, b) \in R_{1} \cup R_{2}$. Then either $(a, b) \in R_{1}$ or $(a, b) \in R_{2}$. In the former case, we have that $(b, a) \in R_{1}$, since $R_{1}$ is symmetric, and in the latter case we have that $(b, a) \in R_{2}$, since $R_{2}$ is symmetric. In either case we have that $(b, a) \in R_{1} \cup R_{2}$.

questions.html:
Let $\text{A, B}$ be two non-empty sets, with cardinality $3,4$ respectively. Let $\text{R}$ be a relation defined on the power set of $\text{A} \times \text{B}.$ Relation $\text{R}$ is reflexive, symmetric, transitive, and antisymmetric. Hence,  Relation $ \text{R}$ is also equivalence relation.

The cardinality of the largest equivalence class of relation $\text{R}$ is?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Selected solution (score: 35)

Detailed Video Solution: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZmfaSa1TKm4&t=5228s (with Complete Analysis) 

Relation $R$ is defined on $P(A\times B)$, i.e., Power set of $A\times B$.

Since, $R$ is reflexive, every element of $P(A\times B)$ is related to itself.

Now, by symmetric and antisymmetric property of $R$, we cannot have $aRb$, such that $a\neq b$.

So, the only element related to $a\in P(A\times B)$, is $a$ itself. So, no two distinct elements of $P(A\times B)$ are related to each other. 

So, each equivalence class which will be formed by $R$ has exactly one element only.

The cardinality of the largest equivalence class of relation $R$ is 1.

NOTE : There is nothing specific about the set $P(A\times B)$ such that this outcome occurred. This will be true for any set, provided that $R$ is Reflexive, Symmetric, Transitive and Anti-Symmetric.

Solution

  1. Base sets
    Let
    $A = {a_1, a_2, a_3}, \quad B = {b_1, b_2, b_3, b_4}$.

  2. Cartesian product
    The Cartesian product is
    $A \times B = {(a_i,b_j) \mid i=1,2,3;\ j=1,2,3,4}$.
    This has $3 \times 4 = 12$ ordered pairs.
    For convenience, label them as
    $A \times B = {p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_{12}}$.

  3. Power set
    The universe of our relation is the power set:
    $S = \mathcal{P}(A \times B) = { X \mid X \subseteq A \times B }$.

    Each element of $S$ is a subset of $A \times B$, possibly of any size between 0 and 12.

    Examples:

    • $X_1 = \varnothing$

    • $X_2 = {p_1}$

    • $X_3 = {p_1,p_5,p_{10}}$

    • $X_4 = {p_2,p_3,\ldots,p_{12}}$

    Total number of subsets:
    $|S| = 2^{12} = 4096$.

  4. Relation $R$
    We are told that $R$ on $S$ is reflexive, symmetric, transitive, and antisymmetric.

    • Reflexive: $X R X$ for all $X \in S$.

    • Symmetric: If $X R Y$ then $Y R X$.

    • Transitive: If $X R Y$ and $Y R Z$, then $X R Z$.

    • Antisymmetric: If $X R Y$ and $Y R X$, then $X=Y$.

  5. Effect of symmetry + antisymmetry
    Take two distinct subsets $X,Y \in S$. Suppose $X R Y$.

    • By symmetry: $Y R X$.

    • By antisymmetry: $X=Y$. Contradiction.

    Hence, no two distinct elements of $S$ can be related.

    Therefore, the only possible pairs in $R$ are of the form $(X,X)$.

  6. Reflexivity ensures
    Because $R$ is reflexive, every $(X,X)$ must be in $R$.
    Thus
    $R = { (X,X) \mid X \in S }$.

    This is exactly the identity relation on $S$.

  7. Equivalence classes
    For any $X \in S$,
    $[X] = { Y \in S \mid X R Y }$.

    But $X$ is related only to itself, so
    $[X] = {X}$.

    Every equivalence class is a singleton set.

  8. Largest equivalence class
    Since all equivalence classes contain exactly one element, the size of the largest equivalence class is
    $1$.

Final Answer: The cardinality of the largest equivalence class of $R$ is
$\boxed{1}$

questions.html: Given a set of values $\text{R} = \{1,2,3,4,5,6,7\}.$ The number of relations on this set which are both partial-order and equivalence relation is?
questions.solution:
Answer: 1

Selected solution (score: 28)

Detailed Video Solution: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZmfaSa1TKm4&t=1761s (with Complete Analysis)  

Answer$: 1$

Let’s understand by taking base set $\text{R} = \{1,2,3,4\}.$

Given a set of values, suppose $\text{R} = \{1,2,3,4\}$ we need to find the number of relations on the set, which are both partial-order and equivalence relations.

Since the relation must be reflexive, it must contain the elements $(1,1),(2,2),(3,3)$, and $(4,4)$. It is not difficult to show (do it if it does not seem clear to you!) that the only relations that are both symmetric and anti-symmetric are identity relations of the form $\{(a, a),(b, b), \ldots\}$. Hence $\{(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(4,4)\}$ is the only relation on the set $\{1,2,3,4\}$ that is reflexive, symmetric, and anti-symmetric. Clearly, it is also transitive, and hence it is the only relation that is both a partial order and an equivalence relation.

The same argument goes for any set $S:$ The only relation that is both a partial order and an equivalence relation is the identity relation $R=\{(x, x) \mid x \in S\}$.

Detailed Video Solution: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZmfaSa1TKm4&t=1761s (with Complete Analysis) 

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Equivalence relation means that the relation should be reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Partial order relation means that the relation should be transitive, anti-symmetric and reflexive. In the matrix representation of relation on set R, we should consider all the pairs along the diagonal as the relation must be reflexive. Number of ways of choosing all of them is 1. For the pairs (a,b) and (b,a) where a is not equal to b, there are four options: i) donot take (a,b) and (b,a), ii) take (a,b) and donot take (b,a), iii) take (b,a) and donot take (a,b), iv) take both of them. Equivalence relation says that only option iv) is allowed. Partial order relation says that option ii) and option iii) are allowed. So if we consider both the cases, we can neither take (a,b) nor (b,a). So final conclusion is that we have to consider all the pairs along the diagonal. We cannot consider any non diagonal pair. Therefore number of relations which are both equivalence and partial order is 1.

questions.html:
Let $\text{R}$ be a relation from a set $\text{A}$ to a set $\text{B}.$ The inverse relation from $\text{B}$ to $\text{A},$ denoted by $\text{R}^{-1},$ is the set of ordered pairs $\{(b,a) \mid (a,b) \in \text{R}\}$.

  • $\text{S1: R}$ is reflexive relation iff $\text{R}^{-1} = \text{R}$
  • $\text{S2: R}$ is a symmetric relation iff $\text{R}^{-1} = \text{R}$

Which one of the following statements is true?
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Selected solution (score: 21)

Detailed Video Solution: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZmfaSa1TKm4&t=2312s (with Complete Analysis) 

S1: $R$ is reflexive relation iff  $R^{-1}=R$

If $R$ is reflexive then $R^{-1}=R$. Is this true?

Let, $A=\{1,2\}$, and  $R=\{(1,1),(2,2),(1,2)\}$. This, $R$ is reflexive but $R^{-1}\neq R$.

So, S1 is False.

S2: $R$ is symmetric iff  $R^{-1}=R$

$\Longrightarrow$ $R$ is symmetric then $R^{-1}=R$.

                 Let, $(a,b)\in R$, then $(b,a)\in R$. Since, $(b,a)\in R$, then $(a,b)\in R^{-1}$. So, $R\subseteq R^{-1}$.

                 Similarly, we can prove $R^{-1}\subseteq R$. Hence, $R=R^{-1}$.

$\Longleftarrow$ $R^{-1}=R$ then $R$ is symmetric.

                Let, $(a,b)\in R$, then $(b,a)\in R^{-1}$. Since, $R^{-1}=R$, so $(b,a)\in R$.

                Thus, $R$ is symmetric.

So, S2 is True.

Detailed Video Solution: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZmfaSa1TKm4&t=2312s (with Complete Analysis) 

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

A  iff B = ( A → B & B → A)

So, to prove A iff B is True we have to show both A→ B and B→ A as True.

But to prove A iff B is False we can show A→ B or B→ A as False.

----------------------------------

S1: R is reflexive relation iff R$^{-1}$ = R

Proof: We can easily disprove it by counter-example.

S1 → if  (R$^{-1}$ = R) then  R is a reflexive relation.

Example  :   Base set A = {a,b} and Relation R = {(a,b),(b,a)}  ,  R$^{-1}$ = {(b,a),(a,b)}

Here, R$^{-1}$ = R but R is not reflexive.

So, S1 is FALSE.

S2: R is a symmetric relation iff  R$^{-1}$ = R

S2 →  if  R$^{-1}$ = R then R is symmetric.

Proof: We can easily prove it by contradiction.

Base set A = {a,b}

S2 → if  (R$^{-1}$ = R) then  R is a symmetric relation. 

suppose, (R$^{-1}$ = R) but R is NOT a symmetric relation.

R$^{-1}$ = R and (a,b) $\epsilon$ R and (b,a) $\notin$ R

(a,b) $\epsilon$ R → (a,b) $\epsilon$ R$^{-1}$ → (b,a)  $\epsilon$ R

so, R is symmetric.

Now, this is not enough to prove S2.

S2 → If  R is symmetric.then  R$^{-1}$ = R.

Proof: We can easily prove it by contradiction.

Base set A = {a,b}

suppose. (a,b) $\epsilon$  R$^{-1}$ and (a,b) $\notin$ R and R is symmetric.

So, (a,b)  $\epsilon$  R$^{-1}$ → (b,a) $\epsilon$  R → (a,b) $\epsilon$  R

So, R=R$^{-1}$

S2 is TRUE.
